title: Fair Credit Reporting Act; Preemption of State Laws
summary:
The federal government announced three notable moves today: the Energy Department updated its clean energy loan guarantee rules, the consumer watchdog said national credit reporting standards generally override state rules, and ocean regulators closed a key pollock fishing area in Alaska for the rest of the year.

At the Energy Department, an interim rule—effective immediately—renames and reshapes part of its loan guarantee program, now called Energy Dominance Financing. The rule broadens what counts as energy infrastructure to include facilities and equipment tied to finding, producing, moving, refining, and generating energy and critical minerals. It also clarifies that projects can repower closed facilities, expand output at operating ones, or support grid reliability. If an electric utility gets a loan guarantee, it must promise to pass the financial benefit to its customers or communities. Developers and utilities could see faster financing for more types of projects, and local ratepayers may share in the savings. Critics may worry the shift in focus and definition could tilt support toward projects they view as less aligned with clean energy goals.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau issued an interpretation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act stating that federal law generally preempts state laws across broad areas of credit reporting. The Bureau withdrew its 2022 view that left more room for state rules and now emphasizes uniform national standards. Credit bureaus, lenders, and companies that supply data may benefit from simpler, nationwide compliance and more consistent reports. Consumers could see easier credit portability across states. On the other hand, states and consumer advocates who want to restrict reporting of items like medical debt, arrest records, or rental arrears may find their options limited, and some consumers may lose protections provided by stricter state rules.

Finally, NOAA closed directed fishing for pollock in one Gulf of Alaska area through year-end to avoid exceeding the annual catch limit. This aims to protect the stock and support long-term sustainability. Fishermen, processors, and local communities may face short-term economic impacts from the shutdown.
